1. The animation shows how paying a mortgage once a year compares with paying monthly. Tessa is an illustrative character with a house. A grid of green tiles stands for the loan's monthly payments. The caption says the math uses the Oct 8, 2026 survey rate. A label says it is "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. The grid starts as a full block of green tiles. In frames 3 and 4, tiles lift out and then turn dark, which looks like payments being used up. The camera then zooms in on the grid. The text "$8,792 once a year (12 × $732.67)" appears, which means one lump payment instead of twelve monthly ones. In the last frame, a few gold tiles sit off the end of the grid, next to the caption "ends in 184 months: 4 months later than monthly."

3. Paying the same total once a year, instead of spreading it across monthly payments, makes the loan finish 4 months later. It ends at 184 months instead of the 180 months of a 15-year loan. Interest accrues while the money waits for the yearly payment, so the loan takes a little longer to clear. The gold tiles are those extra 4 months.

4. A viewer might take this: if you would pay the same total per year anyway, paying monthly is slightly better than paying once a year. The animation does not say whether to pay extra on the mortgage or invest the spare cash. It also gives no rate, balance or investment return to compare. The mortgage in the animation is not shown to match your $320,000.

5. The animation did not suggest this advice. The picture and text only state the 184-month versus 180-month result. The "monthly is better" takeaway is my own conclusion from that result. The "illustrative" and "history, not a forecast" labels point the other way, since they signal that the animation is not meant as advice.
